en: The Arrangement of the Ritual for the Assembly.
Homage to Vajrasattva!
Having paid homage to Vajrasattva,
whose body is indivisible from the three vajras,
[this is] the limb of the sādhana of the Samāja.
The systematic arrangement is now being explained.
First,
one should recite the verse beginning with "abhāva" and so forth.
Sthāvara.
One should cause the objects beginning with form to enter into emptiness;
therein, [one should visualize] that which stands in the midst of the space element.
One should meditate upon the four mandalas, beginning with the wind mandala and so forth.
Having prepared a portion of the ground, one should construct a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) upon it by means of the syllable *bhrūṃ*.
Therein, [one should visualize] Akṣobhya and so forth.
One should resolve that the entire mandala of deities is to be arrayed; then,
through the practice of yoga and its application—
The tri-yoga and mahā-yoga [lead] in sequence to Mahāvajradhara.
Having manifested oneself through the union of the two organs,
one emits the deities of the maṇḍala.
And having performed the meditation upon Japan,
one should perform the dismissal.
The teaching of Nyāsa would thus be indicated.
Now,
the author states the third instruction concerning the systematic arrangement.
When, in this world, the dissolution of the realms has occurred, such that not even a single sentient being remains in the triple world;
Nothing remains;
only the receptacle world persists.
Then, gradually and step by step, (2)
The rays of the seven suns having appeared, they burned the triple world.
They make it consist of space.
The practitioner of the generation stage should contemplate this meaning by means of the verse.
And he focuses upon the Noble Ones once again by the power of the continuity of dependent origination.
The winds blow very gently;
then those winds, increasing in strength, [reach] a depth of sixteen hundred thousand yojanas.
They form an incalculable wind-circle in its circumference above space; upon that wind-circle...
The clouds, having gathered, rain down with streams as thick as axles;
that becomes water.
The maṇḍala; its measurement is eleven hundred thousand yojanas.
Its depth is twenty thousand [yojanas];
furthermore, those waters, being churned by the winds, become golden.
The earth lies above the waters;
its measurement is three hundred thousand [yojanas] in thickness, plus twenty thousand.
The circle of fire, however,
is indeed contained within that;
this is the arising of the configuration.
The yogi should meditate on a wind mandala situated in the center of the space element.
By means of this and other [verses],
one takes hold of the ground through the sequence of the four mandalas.
In this way, having gathered [the elements] by means of winds produced through the power of the karma of sentient beings...
Gold and other substances are made into heaps;
Sumeru and other mountains [are likewise].
The celestial palaces of the gods, the continents, the Cakravāḍa mountain ranges, and the trees, shrubs, creepers, and so forth.
They come into being.
And by this much, the sequence of the arising of existence—
For practitioners, preceded by the characteristic of meditating on emptiness, [it is performed] according to the sequence of the four maṇḍalas.
Having prepared the ground,
one should construct a gabled chamber (kūṭāgāra) upon it; this is what is meant.
Then Mahāvajradhara, the lord of consciousness and the progenitor of beings, [spoke].
Having brought forth the receptacle world,
he constructs the world of sentient beings.
This is because of the statement that the meditation on the generation of the three vajras must be preceded by the accomplishment of the *ālaya*.
In that regard, there are four modes of birth;
therein, [there are those] born from eggs and born from a womb.
"Born from moisture" and "spontaneously born"—
*yoni* means birth.
What is the egg-born mode of birth? It is those sentient beings who are born from eggs, such as:
Swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, and so forth.
What is the womb-born birth (*jarāyuja-yoni*)?
Those beings who are born from a womb,
such as elephants, horses, cows, and buffaloes.
Donkeys, boars, humans, and so forth.
What is the moisture-born birth-place (*saṃsvedajā yoni*)? It refers to those sentient beings who are born from the moisture of the elements.
For example:
worms, insects, moths, mosquitoes, and so forth.
What is the womb of spontaneous birth?
Those beings who are without deficiency...
They are born all at once, with unimpaired faculties and endowed with all major and minor limbs.
For example: gods, hell-beings, those in the intermediate state, the beings of the first eon, and so forth.
To this he says: although humans dwell in all three continents, why is it that those in their final existence (caramabhavika) [are found only here]?
But the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, do not descend there from the excellent realm of Tuṣita.
They will certainly descend here into Jambudvīpa and teach the Dharma to human beings.
May the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Vajra Guru, explain the reason for this.
The Vajra Guru said:
The humans in Pūrvavideha, Aparagodānīya, and Uttarakuru.
They lead to great wealth;
however, they are slow, dull, and characterized by a lack of discernment.
But this Jambudvīpa is the land of karma;
therefore, it is [the place] for good and evil deeds,
whether superior, middling, or inferior.
The ripening of the karmic fruit of sentient beings is seen here;
nevertheless, in this Jambudvīpa, human beings—
Deceitful, hypocritical, intoxicated by pride, and malicious in intent, they are tormented by old age and disease.
But those of illuminated wisdom have sharp faculties; they are of a keen nature.
Therefore, Bodhisattvas are reborn in the various regions of Jambudvīpa.
They teach the Dharma.
Therefore it is said:
"The first treasure is the attainment of human birth."
The attainment of renunciation is the second treasure;
the attainment of going forth is the third treasure;
and the attainment of meditative concentration is the fourth treasure.
Thus it is said; and in the *Asādhāraṇaguhyamahāyogatantra* it is also stated:
The Buddhas of the past, future, and present, having remained in human form, [all]...
They attain the state of omniscience;
for this reason, among human beings...
The stage of generation is now explained:
human beings of the initial eon are adorned with all the qualities of a Buddha.
Possessing form, mind-made,
endowed with all major and minor limbs, and complete.
With unimpaired faculties,
possessing bodies of beautiful complexion, self-luminous,
and traveling through the sky.
Long-lived,
nourished by joy, and embodiments of wisdom,
they [attain] the illusion-like samādhi.
They do not understand;
not understanding, [they remain so] due to the power of the continuous stream of the latencies of ignorance from beginningless time.
Gradually, they are overcome by the karma and afflictions arising from their own minds.
Then, having cast off that mind-made body, they [assume] an ordinary human physical form through the gradual succession of the continuity of afflictions.
In this way, one whose own mind is crooked and who is devoid of spiritual friends grasps [them].
Not knowing their own intrinsic nature, they pass away again and again from the assembly of sentient beings; as long as they do not obtain the necessary conditions, they continue to come back.
He states the certainty that one remains in the intermediate state for at most seven days.
What is the characteristic of the intermediate state?
It is said to exist between the state of death and the state of birth.
That personal existence which arises for the purpose of reaching rebirth in another location is called the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
But he possesses sharp faculties,
just like a Bodhisattva in his final existence who has reached full maturity.
And likewise, even while abiding in the intermediate state, he would enter his mother’s womb possessing all the primary marks and secondary characteristics of an omniscient one.
And a hundred million lamps shine for him,
as it has been said:
In the *Bhadrapāliparipṛcchā-sūtra*: (11) And that man, having dispatched his servant...
He attains divine mindfulness and beholds the gods of the six classes of the desire realm.
He sees the sixteen great hells,
and he sees his own body with symmetrical hands and feet.
And he understands thus:
"Now this is my body.
As it has been said:
In the *Kośakārikā*:
"He is visible to those with pure divine eyes by birth, and possesses the speed of the supernatural power of karma."
Possessing all [senses], unimpeded,
and irreversible, he is called a "Gandharva-eater."
By this, for those who practice the stage of generation, through the sequence of yoga and subsequent application.
The deity, having manifested his perfected form, teaches,
just as a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in his final existence does.
Considering that the benefit of human beings cannot be accomplished by means of the *saṃbhogakāya*,
[he manifests] the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).
By means of this entry, he demonstrates his descent into the womb for the purpose of assuming a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Likewise, even while abiding in the intermediate state (antarābhava),
one does not abandon the continuity of the habitual tendencies of one's own conceptual constructions for seven weeks.
When impelled by the karma of previous existence,
one takes birth through this sequence.
This is the sequence:
Of the humans of the first eon,
who were consuming the food of ambrosia, up until the limit of solid food.
Roughness and heaviness entered his body;
his radiance vanished,
and then darkness arose.
The sun and moon appeared in the world;
from that [arose] the distinction between wisdom and means.
For the purpose of seeing one another,
the female and male faculties appeared among them, and their physical forms became distinct.
As they looked at one another, by the power of previous habituation, a mind of mutual passion arose; from that, they engaged in sexual misconduct. That...
Starting from that, the other designation "woman" and "man" continues to prevail in the world even today;
therefore, he...
Due to the manifestation of three conditions, a gandharva-being enters the mother's womb.
The descent into the womb occurs when the mother is healthy and in her fertile period,
and both the mother and father are filled with desire.
Then, through the empowerment of the diamond of mutual passion between the two, by means of actions such as embracing and kissing, [the union of] the two organs—
Having seen the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*),
[one] abandons the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for the sake of grasping at sense-pleasures (*kāma-upādāna*);
like a horse-rider, consciousness (*vijñāna*) acts as the sovereign.
Cittavajra, mounted upon the wind-vehicle, having arrived most swiftly in a mere instant, a moment, or a muhūrta—
Like a wisdom-being of possession, having entered through the door of Vairocana and attained the stage of gnosis by means of the knowledge of skillful means.
Having become non-dual with him, his heart captivated by unsurpassed joy,
[he beheld] all the Tathāgatas mentioned in the tantras—
According to the method of the *abhibhavana-samādhi*, there are seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*) as stated in the *Prajñāsūtra*.
Having exhorted both of them and satisfied them with the bliss of supreme joy,
Ālikāli, having become one,
entering into the subtle element,
both [arise] from the emergence of the rays of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*).
Having been liquefied and becoming thoroughly mixed with the semen and blood, it falls into the middle of the womb in the form of a drop.
Illuminating this meaning, it is said in the *Mūlatantra*:
"The heart of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas..."
The vajra wanders within the wombs of women;
from that, it gradually increases.
First is the form of the *kalala*;
from the *kalala* arises the *arbuda*; from the *arbuda* arises the *peśī*.
From the *peśī* is born the *ghana*;
from the *ghana*, moreover, being impelled by the wind,
the fivefold branches arise.
Blister-like forms arise;
from that, the hair of the head, body hair, nails, and so forth, as well as the sense organs and physical forms, are produced.
Regarding the phrase "the consonants in successive order": through the empowerment of the five Tathāgatas, that [syllable] reaches the state of the seed-syllable (bīja).
Having begun, it arises in five forms:
here, the *kalala* belongs to Akṣobhya,
and the *arbuda* belongs to Ratnasaṃbhava.
The flesh belongs to Amitābha;
the bone to Amoghasiddhi;
the tendons to Vairocana.
Regarding the term "adhisthāna":
it shows even one who is intensely passionate the fivefold form.
In that regard, the fluid belongs to Akṣobhya,
the blood to Amitābha,
and the embryo to Ratnasaṃbhava.
The dense [state] of Amoghasiddhi is the combined empowerment of Vairocana.
There are two channels in the middle of the womb,
likewise on the left and the right;
one should know that the semen is in the left.
And on the right, red alone;
the merging of those two into oneness is their own inclusion within the *dharmadhātu*.
Thus.
Therefore, after some time,
for that [mind] which has reached maturity, like a seed and its sprout, [it arises].
Within the womb, inside the mother's belly, winds born from the ripening of karma blow.
Those who, having turned the fetus within the womb, face the opening of the source of phenomena (dharmodaya) at their mother’s belly;
They establish [the embryo];
if it is to be a male,
it remains resting against the mother's right flank.
Facing his back,
he remains in a squatting position;
then, if it is a woman, [he enters] the left side of the womb.
Having taken hold [of it], it turns toward the abdomen;
then, at the end of ten months,
as stated in the Mūlasūtra—
In order to demonstrate the vajra-samādhi arising from the pledge (samaya), he emerged from his mother’s womb.
Therefore, that Gandharva-being becomes visible to the fleshly eye.
And for this reason, it is said in the Root Sūtra:
The Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bodhicittavajra, appeared in the form of three faces together with all the Tathāgatas.
"It was seen," it is said.
Regarding this, he says:
"The water element is to be known as paternal."
The fire element is maternal;
skin, flesh, and blood are said to be maternal.
The sinews, marrow, [and] semen are said to be paternal;
these are declared to be the maternal constituents.
And the aggregates that comprise the person:
namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"The universe consists of the five Buddhas; these are called the aggregates (skandhas) and so forth.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One to the four goddesses.
In the *Paripṛcchā-mahāyoga-tantra*,
by means of this much of the text, the practitioner should cultivate the pride of thinking, "I am one who has perfected the four yogas."
"It should be generated."
[The second section on the teaching:
The establishment of the generation stage.]
First Chapter.
[1] Now he states the third instruction concerning the established order.
First,
the body-maṇḍala is established,
beginning with the Brahma-thread.
Quadrangular in its divisions,
it appears like a gabled chamber.
The characteristic of the body of yogins is called "bhaga," which is the mandala;
and the bodhicitta is the mandala.
"The body is said to be the maṇḍala; thus is the threefold conceptualization of the maṇḍala," according to the statement in the *Samājottara* (20).
Thus, within the maṇḍala of one's own body,
by way of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
He explains the relationship of cause and effect among the deities assigned [to the aggregates].
Therein, regarding the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha):
Vairocana;
Ratnasaṃbhava in the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha).
Perception is Amitābha;
mental formations are Amoghasiddhi;
consciousness is Akṣobhya.
Therefore, it is said in the Mūlasūtra:
"In brief, the five aggregates are proclaimed as the five Buddhas."
Therefore, having understood the specific characteristics of the aggregates through the arrangement of the five Tathāgatas, [one should proceed].
The five aggregates become the causes of awakening,
as it is said in the *Mūlasūtra*: "Hatred, delusion, and likewise passion..."
Likewise, these five families, which consist of wish-fulfilling gems,
are indeed the accomplishers of both desire and liberation.
Thus [it is said].
He states the arrangement of the deities:
Locanā is delight in delusion;
she is the earth element.
Māmakī, who delights in hatred, is the water element; Pāṇḍaravāsinī delights in passion.
The fire element is Vajrarati; Tārā is the wind element.
Illuminating this point, he says in the Root Sūtra: "The earth is known as Locanā."
The water element is known as Māmakī;
fire is called Pāṇḍarā;
and wind is proclaimed to be Tārā.
Thus,
having also understood the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of these elements (dhātu).
The elements, through the arrangement of the deities, become bestowers of Buddhahood;
[namely] the sense-bases of the eye and so forth—
He states the cause and effect of the Bodhisattvas who have been thus arranged:
that very Blessed One is Cittavajra.
Abiding in the eye faculty through the Kṣitigarbha-samādhi, one perceives the threefold form.
Having ascertained it through its luminosity, he bestows the faculty of the vajra-eye.
In this way, Vajrapāṇi,
abiding in the faculty of hearing,
likewise discerns the three kinds of sound.
Ākāśagarbha bestows the adamantine faculty of hearing. (23)
Abiding in the olfactory faculty and having discerned the three fragrances,
he bestows the vajra-olfactory faculty.
Lokeśvara, abiding in the faculty of the tongue, having discerned the three tastes,
bestows the vajra-tongue faculty.
The Blessed One Mañjuśrī, abiding in the six evolving consciousnesses, having examined the three types of knowledge, [spoke].
The Blessed One bestows the supernormal knowledge of knowing the minds of others.
Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin,
abiding in the faculty of the body,
caused the hindrances to disappear.
Having mutually condensed them and entered into the state of birth, one brings about the vajra-body.
The Blessed One Samantabhadra,
remaining everywhere at the point of the joint,
[attained] the luminous joint.
The Blessed Maitreya, remaining in the nature of sinews, bestows [it].
Having bound it with tendons,
he causes it to enter the *prabhāsvara*.
That very Blessed One, having manifested in the form of the three bodies as if external,
Because she bestows the pleasure of the eye-faculty, she is Rūpavajrā;
likewise for Śabdavajrā and the others as well.
It should be understood.
For the Blessed One, Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata, is indeed the union of all;
his enjoyment is indeed everything.
"Entirely from the three realms," because of the statement regarding restraint;
by this placement of the deities.
By means of the thorough knowledge of intrinsic nature,
one brings about the purification of the object;
illustrating this point:
It is said in the *Mūlasūtra*:
"The vajra-spheres themselves are the supreme maṇḍala of the bodhisattvas."
Thus,
the practitioner of mantra should always meditate upon the deity by means of forms, sounds, and so forth. (25)
Thus [it is said].
He explains the cause and effect for those who have directed their wrath toward the individual limbs:
Yamāntaka is on the right arm.
Aparājita is on the left side;
Hayagrīva should be visualized at the mouth,
and Amṛtakuṇḍalin at the thunderbolt.
One should contemplate Acala on the right arm and Ṭakkirājaka on the left,
and [Acala] upon the right knee.
The great blazing Nīladaṇḍa on the left knee, and Mahābala on the head,
as well as Uṣṇīṣacakrin.
One should contemplate Sumbharāja placed at the two ends of the feet.
These ten wrathful kings,
when placed upon the limbs of the practitioner, act spontaneously and without effort.
Having emerged from the body-maṇḍala in the form of one with three faces and six arms, [he subdues] the hosts of obstructors in the ten directions.
They threaten.
Therefore, it is said in the *Mūlasūtra*: "Born from the abode of anger and hatred,
they are constantly intent on killing."
They are accomplished for the purpose of slaying by the practitioner who possesses the supreme dharma.
The third chapter: The Arrangement of the Body Mandala.
The mantra-practitioner, having realized both the cause and the fruit of the deities arrayed in the body-maṇḍala,
[proceeds] for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others.
One emanates the emanation-maṇḍala from the body-maṇḍala by means of this sequence.
This is the sequence:
Having mentally expanded [the visualization] of one's own family woman,
or else having taken an external woman,
according to the sequence described in the *Sādhana*.
Having brought about the union of the two organs,
from the *bodhicitta*— just as [from one celestial palace]— (27) [half].
Having constructed the peaked pavilion according to the previously stated sequence,
[one recites] the mantra beginning with "Vajradhrk."
Having recited the entire circle of deities, one should create them;
this is the rule for the mantra of emission.
He said:
"The vajra symbolizes the fivefold manifest enlightenment."

by this, having purified the affliction of hatred—
Having returned once more, he became non-dual with Mahāvajradhara.

thus, in twelve aspects—

He wears the jewel that fulfills all [wishes].

the vajra has the five wisdoms as its intrinsic nature.

Space is unobstructed gnosis;
that itself is the womb (garbha), thus he is Ākāśagarbha.

Mañjuśrī,

Samantabhadra:
That by which one is affected or reflected is form (*rūpa*);
that which is sounded is sound (*śabda*).
That which is smelled is odor (*gandha*). That which is tasted is flavor (*rasa*). That which is touched is tangibility (*sparśa*).
Through the proximity of the word "vajra" and by means of that meditative absorption,

Yama is hell; that Blessed One [subdues it] through the samādhi of great wrath.
He makes an end [to Yama], thus he is Yamāntakṛt;
he makes an end to bonds by means of wisdom, thus he is Prajñāntakṛt.
By means of the analogy of the lotus,
he brings an end to those with pure passion; thus, he is the "Lotus-End-Maker" (Padmāntakṛt).
The four Māras are the obstacles; that Blessed One, by means of the samādhi of great wrath, [subdues them].
He is called Vighnāntakṛt because he brings an end to those [obstacles].
He constantly [transcends] the eight worldly conventions.

Ṭakki is desire. He is so called because he rules, illuminates, and purifies.
Ṭakkirāja: the blue [deity] who [destroys] the evil of sentient beings.

The Tathāgatas Akṣobhya, Ratna, Amitābha, Amogha, and Vairocana.
